opus-5.5.text:
I think the VLA framing has been really useful, but it's also a bit of a trap if we take it too literally. Right now the common recipe is: take a big pretrained vision-language model, bolt on an action head, and fine-tune on robot demonstrations. That gets you surprisingly far on semantic generalization. The robot can understand "pick up the thing you'd use to drink coffee" even if it's never seen that exact mug. But the bottleneck isn't really the language part anymore. It's the physical part.

So I'd say a few directions matter.

First, the action side needs to be taken much more seriously. Language models are built for discrete tokens and fairly slow reasoning, while manipulation is continuous, high-frequency, and contact-rich. That's why people moved toward diffusion or flow-matching action experts, and toward splitting the system into something like a slow "thinking" module and a fast "reacting" module. I think that hierarchy, a high-level planner running at a few hertz and a low-level controller running much faster, will become standard rather than one monolithic model doing everything at one rate.

Second, the representations have to carry more physics. Vision-language pretraining tells you what objects are and what they're called, but not how heavy they are, how they deform, or what happens when you push them. So I'm excited about bringing in video prediction and world models, and about adding modalities like force, touch, and proprioception as first-class inputs rather than afterthoughts. A model that can imagine the consequences of its actions is much more robust than one that just pattern-matches from observation to action.

Third, data. Everyone knows robot data is scarce, but I think the interesting question is what *kind* of data scales. Teleoperation is high quality but expensive. Human videos are abundant but lack action labels and embodiment match. Simulation is cheap but has the sim-to-real gap. The architectures that win will probably be the ones designed to absorb all three, with different parts of the model learning from different sources, rather than ones that only consume perfectly paired robot trajectories.

And finally, I'd like to see VLAs get better at learning after deployment. Today they're mostly trained once and frozen. But a real robot in a home or factory should get better from its own failures, from corrections, maybe from reinforcement learning on top of the pretrained policy. That closed loop is where I think the next big jump comes from, more than just making the backbone bigger.

So in short: less "a language model that outputs actions," more "an embodied model that happens to understand language."

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll give you my honest take, which is that I think the current VLA paradigm is a very good first step and also something we'll look back on as a bit naive.

Let me explain what I mean. Right now, most VLA work takes a pretrained vision-language model, bolts on an action head, and fine-tunes on robot demonstration data. That works surprisingly well for getting a robot to follow instructions in settings that look like the training data. But it has a few structural problems that I think define where the field needs to go.

The first is the data bottleneck. Language models got to where they are because the internet handed them trillions of tokens for free. Robot action data doesn't exist at that scale, and teleoperation is expensive and slow. So the question becomes: where does the action-relevant signal come from? I think the answer has to be some combination of large-scale human video, simulation, and the robot's own autonomous experience. Human video is interesting because it's abundant and it encodes intent and physical reasoning, but the embodiment gap is real. You have to learn a representation of "what is happening in the world" that transfers across bodies before you learn "what my particular arm should do." That argues for a more layered architecture, where there's a world-understanding layer that's embodiment-agnostic and a thinner control layer that's specific to the hardware.

The second issue is that most VLAs today are essentially reactive. They map the current observation to the next action chunk. There's not much explicit planning, not much reasoning about consequences, and not much memory. For short tabletop tasks that's fine. For a robot that has to tidy an apartment over twenty minutes, it isn't. I think we'll see architectures that separate a slower deliberative process, which can be the language model reasoning about subgoals, from a fast reactive controller that handles contact and precision. Humans clearly work this way. The interesting research question is how those two layers communicate, and whether the interface is language, latent plans, or something else.

The third thing is that I'm skeptical actions should be tokenized the same way language is. Discretizing continuous control into vocabulary tokens was a convenient hack to reuse the transformer machinery. Diffusion and flow-matching action heads are already showing that continuous, multimodal action distributions matter for dexterity. I expect the action side of the architecture to diverge more and more from the language side.

And then there's the uncomfortable question of what "vision-language" even buys you. The language part is valuable for instruction following and for inheriting commonsense priors. But I suspect a lot of the physical competence will end up coming from world models, from predicting what the world looks like after you act, not from captioned images. So in five years the acronym might be something like vision-world-action, with language as an interface rather than the core.

If I had to compress it: VLAs should get more hierarchical, more grounded in prediction and physical experience rather than only imitation, and more honest about the fact that control is not language. The teams that figure out the data engine, meaning how robots generate their own useful training signal in the real world, are the ones that will win, more than the teams with the cleverest architecture diagram.

astra-6.text:
I think the next step is to make the connection between perception, reasoning, and action much tighter. A system can describe what it sees very well and still struggle to act on it. For robotics, the real question is: does it understand enough about the situation to choose an action, observe the result, and adjust?

I’d like to see architectures that support different timescales. You need high-level reasoning about goals, but you also need fast, continuous control. You don’t want every small correction of a robot’s hand to require a long reasoning process. The challenge is to connect those levels so that the controller can respond quickly and the planner can reconsider when something unexpected happens.

I also think we should move beyond treating vision and language as the whole input. Touch, force, and the robot’s own body state matter. If you’re picking up a cup, seeing it isn’t enough—you need to know whether you have a stable grip.

And finally, these models need to handle uncertainty better. When should they act, when should they gather more information, and when should they ask for help? To me, progress means becoming more reliable in that whole loop, especially when the environment differs from the training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next step for VLA architectures is to move from mapping observations and instructions directly to actions toward systems that can understand how their actions change the world.

A robot needs more than the ability to recognize an object and reach for it. It needs to anticipate what might happen when it makes contact, detect when its prediction was wrong, and adjust. So I would put a lot of emphasis on memory, predictive models, and closed-loop control. Vision and language are useful, but touch and information about the robot’s own movement also matter, especially for manipulation.

There’s also a question of timescale. Understanding a request like ‘clean up the table’ involves planning over minutes, while keeping a glass from slipping requires a very fast response. I think architectures should accommodate those different timescales without requiring one large model to handle every control decision.

And we should judge progress by how well these systems recover from mistakes and generalize to unfamiliar situations. A successful demonstration is encouraging, but reliable behavior across changing objects, environments, and instructions is the more meaningful test.
